original_question: Let {P_n(x)} be an orthogonal polynomial sequence satisfying the three-term recurrence P_n(x) = (x-c_n)P_{n-1}(x) - lambda_n P_{n-2}(x) with P_{-1}(x)=0, P_0(x)=1, real c_n, positive lambda_n, c_n -> infinity, and lambda_{n+1}/(c_n c_{n+1}) -> 1/4. If x_{n,1} < ... < x_{n,n} are the zeros of P_n, xi_i = lim_{n->infinity} x_{n,i}, eta_j = lim_{n->infinity} x_{n,n-j+1}, sigma = lim_{i->infinity} xi_i, and tau = lim_{j->infinity} eta_j, then in the one-quarter class one has tau = infinity and the hardest remaining case is sigma = -infinity. What is the correct analogue of Blumenthal's theorem in this sigma = -infinity case?
target_in_paper: Section 2, "Blumenthal–Nevai theorems for the one quarter class of orthogonal polynomials": the unnumbered open question in the final paragraph, "Is there an analog of Blumenthal’s theorem for this case?", referring specifically to the one-quarter-class case σ = -∞ after τ = ∞ and the finite-σ and σ = ∞ cases have been discussed. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper very closely: it uses the exact three-term recurrence, the one-quarter-class hypotheses lim c_n = ∞ and lim λ_{n+1}/(c_n c_{n+1}) = 1/4, the same zero notation x_{n,1} < ⋯ < x_{n,n}, ξ_i, η_j, σ, τ, and it correctly isolates σ = -∞ as the remaining hard case after noting τ = ∞. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
missing_details: The paper states this as an open problem, not as a theorem with a known answer; the official wording is the question "Is there an analog of Blumenthal’s theorem for this case?" ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

To make the question fully stand-alone, you should spell out what "analog of Blumenthal’s theorem" is asking for: Blumenthal’s classical theorem is a zero-density statement, namely that the zeros of all P_n are dense in [σ, τ]; in the present σ = -∞, τ = ∞ setting, the sharpened target is to determine the closure of the union of all zeros, with density in ℝ as the natural candidate. The paper itself asks for the analogue but does not state the answer. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

The scope should remain the one-quarter class of real orthogonal polynomial sequences / corresponding Jacobi matrices only; the ambient setting is the real line, with c_n real and λ_n > 0. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

For paper-faithfulness, the Blumenthal question should not be conflated with the separate Nevai-type spectral question. Section 2 explicitly treats zero-density and essential spectrum as different issues, and says the essential-spectrum problem for finite σ was later settled under an additional monotonicity condition. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

A useful nearby contextual detail omitted by the draft is that the paper emphasizes the scarcity of examples: it says the only known OPS of this type is the Meixner polynomials of the second kind (Meixner–Pollaczek). ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
refined_question: Let {P_n}_{n≥0} be a real orthogonal polynomial sequence defined by P_{-1}(x)=0, P_0(x)=1, and P_n(x)=(x-c_n)P_{n-1}(x)-λ_n P_{n-2}(x) for n≥1, where c_n∈ℝ, λ_n>0, lim_{n→∞} c_n=∞, and lim_{n→∞} λ_{n+1}/(c_n c_{n+1})=1/4. If x_{n,1}<⋯<x_{n,n} are the zeros of P_n, define ξ_i=lim_{n→∞}x_{n,i}, η_j=lim_{n→∞}x_{n,n-j+1}, σ=lim_{i→∞}ξ_i, and τ=lim_{j→∞}η_j; in this one-quarter class τ=∞. In the unresolved case σ=-∞, determine the correct analogue of Blumenthal’s theorem: what is the closure of the set of all zeros of the polynomials P_n, and in particular are these zeros dense in the whole real line ℝ? ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
justification: Section 2 is the only place in arXiv:1607.06196 matching your hypotheses and notation. Your draft reproduces the setup almost verbatim from that section, including the one-quarter-class limit λ_{n+1}/(c_n c_{n+1})→1/4, the zero limits ξ_i, η_j, σ, τ, the fact τ=∞, and the statement that σ=-∞ is the remaining difficult case. The paper then explicitly asks, without giving a solution, whether there is an analogue of Blumenthal’s theorem in this case; it separately notes that the finite-σ essential-spectrum problem is another question and had been settled under an added monotonicity assumption. That is why the refined question should stay narrowly on the σ=-∞ zero-distribution problem rather than being rewritten as a general spectral or existence problem, though the neighboring remark about Meixner–Pollaczek gives the relevant context. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
